title: Individualized Education Program (IEP) draft
summary: A draft individualized education program prepared for the IEP team meeting: present levels of performance, measurable annual goals with baselines, how progress is measured and reported, services with start date, frequency, location and duration, participation with peers, assessment accommodations and, where due, transition planning. The team, including the parent, adopts or changes it.
audience: The IEP team: the parents, general and special education teachers, related service providers, an agency representative, the student when appropriate, and the case manager who prepares the draft for the meeting.
tone: Plain, specific and respectful: concrete, observable language a parent can check, person-first wording, strengths stated alongside needs, and every proposal worded as a proposal.
preamble: You are helping a case manager draft parts of an individualized education program (IEP) before the team meets. This is a DRAFT for the IEP team, which includes the parent; the team develops and adopts the IEP at the meeting and may change any part of it, so word goals, services and placements as proposals ("proposed", "for the team to consider"), never as decisions already made. Do not diagnose and do not decide eligibility: take the student's eligibility, evaluation results and needs from the material. Use federal (IDEA) terms; state forms, committee names and any state-specific requirements come from the requirement set the team uses. Ground every present level, baseline and need in a dated source (evaluation report, progress data, assessment results, teacher or parent input) and name it. Write measurable goals: a condition, an observable behavior, a criterion and a time frame within one year, with a baseline on the same measure and unit as the criterion; avoid verbs that cannot be observed (understand, improve, appreciate). Never invent scores, dates, minutes or service amounts: where one is missing write a placeholder such as "[baseline needed]" or "[minutes per week]". Refer to the student as "[Student]" or by the first name already in the material, and add no identifying details beyond those already there.

sections.heading: IEP Information
sections.guidance: Front matter the case manager fills in: placeholders for the student and the meeting, the purpose of the meeting, the IEP dates and the team members by role. It marks the document as a draft so no one mistakes it for the adopted IEP. Not drafted by the model.
elements: Draft status stated
Student placeholders, grade and eligibility category from the evaluation
Meeting purpose (initial, annual, revision) and date
Proposed IEP start and end dates
Team members by role, including the parent
dataNeeded: Meeting date and proposed IEP dates

sections.heading: Present Levels of Academic Achievement and Functional Performance
sections.guidance: Describe where the student is now in each area of need, drawing on the most recent evaluation, current classroom and progress data, state and district assessments, and teacher and parent input. For each area (for example reading, written expression, math, communication, behavior, motor, daily living), give current performance with dated data on a named measure, the student's strengths, and how the disability affects involvement and progress in the general curriculum (for a preschool child, in age-appropriate activities). Include the parent's concerns for enhancing the student's education in their own terms. End each area with the specific need it shows, since every annual goal will trace back to a need here. Common failures: present levels copied unchanged from last year's IEP or the evaluation; data with no date or measure; needs that no data supports; no strengths.
sections.lengthHint: A short paragraph or list per area of need
elements: Current performance in each area of need, with dated data on a named measure
Student strengths
How the disability affects involvement and progress in the general curriculum
Parent concerns for the student's education
Results of the most recent evaluation, summarized
A specific need stated for each area
sourcesNeeded: Progress-monitoring data and progress reports on the current IEP
dataNeeded: Current scores or data points by area, with dates

sections.heading: Special Factors
sections.guidance: Record what the team should consider for each special factor, with the evidence: whether behavior impedes the student's learning or that of others (and, if so, the positive behavioral interventions and supports proposed, or a link to the behavior intervention plan); the language needs of a student with limited English proficiency; Braille for a student who is blind or visually impaired; communication needs, including language and communication mode for a student who is deaf or hard of hearing; and assistive technology devices and services. Say "not indicated by the data" where a factor does not apply rather than leaving it out, and leave the decision on each to the team.
sections.lengthHint: One line or short paragraph per factor
elements: Behavior: whether it impedes learning, with positive behavioral supports proposed if so
Language needs for a student with limited English proficiency
Braille for a student who is blind or visually impaired
Communication needs and mode
Assistive technology devices and services
sourcesNeeded: Behavior data or functional behavior assessment, where relevant

sections.heading: Proposed Annual Goals
sections.guidance: Propose one or more measurable annual goals for each need in the present levels, academic and functional. Write each goal with four parts: the condition (given what, in what setting), the observable behavior, the criterion (how well, how often, on what measure) and the time frame (by a date within one year). State the baseline beside each goal on the same measure and unit as the criterion, and make sure the target is above the baseline. Number the goals and name the need each addresses. For a student who takes an alternate assessment aligned to alternate achievement standards, add benchmarks or short-term objectives. If a need gets no goal (for example because an accommodation meets it), say so with the reason. Common failures: verbs that cannot be observed; a target at or below the baseline; baseline and target in different units; a goal carried over unchanged with no new data; several skills crammed into one goal.
sections.lengthHint: Usually 2–6 goals, each 1–3 sentences with its baseline
elements: One or more goals per need, each naming the need it addresses
Condition, observable behavior, criterion and a date within one year in each goal
Baseline on the same measure and unit as the criterion
Target above the baseline
Benchmarks or short-term objectives for a student who takes alternate assessments
Reason stated for any need with no goal
sourcesNeeded: Present levels and the data behind them
Progress data on last year's goals

sections.heading: Measuring and Reporting Progress
sections.guidance: For each goal, say how progress will be measured (the tool or method, who collects it, how often) and when the parent will receive periodic progress reports (for example each grading period, with report cards). The measure should be the one the goal's criterion uses, so reports compare like with like. A table works well: goal number, measure, collected by, frequency, reported to parent.
sections.lengthHint: A short table or one line per goal
elements: Measurement method for each goal, matching its criterion
Who collects the data and how often
When progress reports go to the parent

sections.heading: Proposed Services, Aids and Supports
sections.guidance: List the proposed special education services, related services, supplementary aids and services, program modifications and supports for school personnel, each tied to the goals or needs it serves. For every service give the projected start date and the anticipated frequency, location and duration in a table (service, goals served, start date, frequency, location, duration, provider role). Include classroom accommodations here or in their own list. Prefer supports with a research base where the sources name one. Keep amounts as placeholders unless the material gives them, and word everything as proposed for the team's decision. Common failures: a goal with no service behind it; "as needed" in place of a frequency; services with no location.
sections.lengthHint: A service table plus a short accommodations list
elements: Special education services with the goals each serves
Related services, where indicated
Supplementary aids, accommodations and program modifications
Supports for school personnel
Start date, frequency, location and duration for every service
dataNeeded: Proposed minutes, frequency and location for each service

sections.heading: Participation with Peers
sections.guidance: Explain the extent, if any, to which the student would not take part with nondisabled peers in the regular class and in extracurricular and nonacademic activities under the proposed services, and why, in terms of the student's needs. Describe the supports that let the student take part where they do. The team decides placement; present the proposal and the reasons, not a conclusion.
elements: Time or settings away from nondisabled peers, if any
The reason for any removal, tied to the student's needs
Supports for participation in regular classes and activities

sections.heading: State and District Assessments
sections.guidance: Propose how the student takes part in state and districtwide assessments: the individual accommodations needed (consistent with those used in instruction), or, when an alternate assessment is proposed, why the student cannot take the regular assessment and why the alternate one is appropriate. Take the list of allowed accommodations from the state's current assessment policy, not from memory.
elements: Assessment accommodations, consistent with instructional accommodations
If an alternate assessment is proposed, why the regular one is not suitable and why the alternate one is

sections.heading: Transition Planning
sections.guidance: Include when the IEP will be in effect when the student turns 16, or earlier if the team or state requires it. Propose measurable postsecondary goals for training or education, employment and, where appropriate, independent living, each based on age-appropriate transition assessments named with their dates, and the transition services and course of study that support them. Note that the student is invited to the meeting and how the student's preferences and interests were gathered. Beginning at least a year before the state's age of majority, include the statement that the student has been told of the rights that will transfer.
sections.lengthHint: A short list of postsecondary goals and services
elements: Measurable postsecondary goals (education or training, employment, independent living where appropriate)
Age-appropriate transition assessments named and dated
Transition services and course of study
Student preferences and interests, and how they were gathered
Transfer-of-rights statement when within a year of the age of majority
dataNeeded: Student's age at the IEP start date

rubric.criterion: Measurable goals: each goal has a condition, an observable behavior, a criterion and a date within a year, with a baseline on the same measure.

levels.descriptor: Every goal has all four parts, an observable verb, a baseline on the same measure and unit as the criterion, and a target above the baseline.
Goals are measurable, but one lacks a baseline, mixes units, or bundles more than one skill.
Several goals use verbs that cannot be observed, lack a criterion or date, or set a target at or below the baseline.
Goals are general aims ("will improve reading") that no one could measure.

rubric.criterion: Needs to goals to services: every need in the present levels leads to a goal (or a stated reason for none), and every goal has a documented need and a service behind it.

levels.descriptor: The trace holds in both directions: each need maps to a goal or a reason, each goal names its need and is served by at least one listed service.
One need lacks a goal or reason, or one goal lacks a clear service.
Several needs go unaddressed, or goals appear with no need in the present levels.
Goals and services bear no visible relation to the present levels.

rubric.criterion: Current, dated data: present levels and baselines rest on named, dated measures and current input, not last year's text.

levels.descriptor: Every present level and baseline cites a named measure and date from the current period; strengths and parent concerns are included; nothing is carried over unchanged.
Mostly current and dated; one area relies on general description or older data.
Present levels are largely narrative with few data points, or repeat the evaluation or last IEP.
No data; present levels are impressions.

rubric.criterion: Service details: each service has a start date, frequency, location, duration and provider role.

levels.descriptor: Every service, aid and modification lists all of start date, frequency, location and duration, with placeholders where the amount is still to be set.
One service lacks a detail, or uses a vague amount.
Several services use "as needed" or omit location or duration.
Services are named with no details.

rubric.criterion: A draft for the team: proposals are worded as proposals, and the parent's part in deciding is preserved.

levels.descriptor: The document is labelled a draft; goals, services and placement are worded as proposals; parent concerns appear; nothing reads as decided before the meeting.
Labelled a draft, but a few statements read as settled ("will receive").
Large parts read as final decisions, or parent input is absent.
Presented as a finished, adopted IEP.
